knowledge_point.title: Computing Gradient of a Quadratic Function

question.:question/problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{3}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}x $$ with respect to $x$ at $$ \displaystyle x={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}. $$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix},
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $$
\displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}:
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2-2 \\ 2-2 \\ 2-6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing Fundamental Matrices Using Matrix Exponentials

question.:question/problem:
$$ A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} $$ Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.
${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{2t}t \\  & =t{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((2\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(2\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(2\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+2\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2y(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(1) \\ y(1)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: $$ \displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}, $$ where $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}. $$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$ So, the matrix of the system is $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2(t-1)} & (t-1){e}^{2(t-1)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-1)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\,{e}^{2(t-1)}\, \\ \,0\,\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 15\end{bmatrix} \\  & =3\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =3v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=3v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=3.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
From the given information, we have 

$$
T\cdot v=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We need to reverse the action of the matrix $T.$ So, we multiply the above equation by ${T}^{-1},$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}\cdot T\cdot v & ={T}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\ v & ={T}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to calculate the inverse of $T$, which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{20-16}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 8 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 8 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the original vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v & ={T}^{-1}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 8 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating a Matrix Polynomial

question.:question/problem:

$f(A)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the polynomial, interpreting any constants as multiples of the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(X) & ={X}^{2}+1 \\  & ={X}^{2}+I\end{aligned}
$$

So, we want to find $f(A)={A}^{2}+I.$

Let's calculate ${A}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can evaluate $f(A):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{2}+I \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1+1 & 0+0 \\ 0+0 & -1+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-5\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((5\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(5\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(5\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+5\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(5t) &={e}^{5t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(5t) &={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{5t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{5t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
5t{e}^{5t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}(1-5t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5{e}^{5t}t+{e}^{5t}(1-5t) \\  & ={e}^{5t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{5t}t \\  & =t{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((3\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(3\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(3\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+3\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & =3\cdot \frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=3t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(t) &={e}^{t} \\ r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t} \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{t}}{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{3{e}^{t}-{e}^{3t}}{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{t}}{2t}\cdot t+\frac{3{e}^{t}-{e}^{3t}}{2} \\  & ={e}^{t} \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =3\cdot \frac{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{t}}{2t}\cdot t+\frac{3{e}^{t}-{e}^{3t}}{2} \\  & ={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-t

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-t) &={e}^{-t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-t) &={e}^{-t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{-t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-t}.

$$
-t{e}^{-t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-t}(1+t).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-{e}^{-t}t+{e}^{-t}(1+t) \\  & ={e}^{-t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{-t}t \\  & =t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.

$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$ {{field-1}}

question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-3)}\,x(3) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4(t-3)} & (t-3){e}^{4(t-3)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-3)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\,-{e}^{4(t-3)}\, \\ \,0\,\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}

question.:question/worked-solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $$
\displaystyle x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}:
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2+1+1 \\ 1+2-2 \\ 1-2+2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-t)={e}^{-t} \\ r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-t}}{3t}.

$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing Gradient of a Quadratic Function

question.:question/problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{3}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 3 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}x $$ with respect to $x$ at $x={\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}.$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 3 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 3 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 4 & 4 \\ 4 & 0 & -2 \\ 4 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 4 & 4 \\ 4 & 0 & -2 \\ 4 & -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0+4-4 \\ 0+0+2 \\ 0-2-2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
